picked.t: China foreign arrivals rise 15.6% amid visa-free push
picked.body: According to National Immigration Administration figures released on Oct. 20, almost four in five foreign arrivals entered without a visa. Vietnam was the third largest source of foreign visitors during the quarter, behind Russia and South Korea, the South China Morning Post reported. Beijing has been expanding visa-free access to attract more international visitors and boost tourism spending. What began as a trial for six nationalities in 2023 had expanded to 50 countries by September 2026, with the visitors now allowed to stay for up to 30 days, Xinhua reported. A separate transit scheme allows travelers passing through China on their way to another destination to stay for up to 10 days without a visa. The push also addresses practical difficulties visitors can face after arrival, from paying for purchases to navigating services in another language. Under the five-year tourism development plan approved by the State Council, authorities aim to make payments, transport and accommodation more convenient for overseas visitors. Other measures include improving shopping tax refunds and expanding multilingual assistance. The plan also calls for more international flights and rail connections, linking easier entry with better access to destinations across the country. China aims to attract 190 million inbound tourists a year by 2030, and turn growing interest in visiting the country into greater tourism spending.

picked.t: Vietnam set to overtake Southeast Asia's largest economy in GDP per capita this year
picked.body: The figures, from the IMF's October World Economic Outlook, put Vietnam's nominal output per person 8.9% above last year's level and nearly double what it was a decade earlier. Vietnam trailed Indonesia by about $250 last year, IMF estimates show, and the fund's April outlook had still projected Indonesia staying ahead in 2026. The new projections would make Vietnam fifth among ASEAN members, behind Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia and Thailand. The IMF expects it to keep its lead over Indonesia in 2027, at $5,659 against $5,550. Indonesia remains Southeast Asia's largest economy by far. With nearly three times Vietnam's population of just over 100 million, its GDP is projected at $1.48 trillion this year, against Vietnam's $542 billion. Nikkei Asia linked the shift to Vietnam's growing role in high-tech manufacturing of semiconductors and electronics, noting that Taiwan's Foxconn is expanding production there. South Korea's Samsung Electronics makes smartphones and other electronics for export at its northern Vietnamese factories. Vietnam's economy grew 9.95% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in four years. The government's public investment push is also supporting growth, Mai Fujita, a senior research fellow at Japan's Institute of Developing Economies, told Nikkei Asia . Vietnam plans to spend VND1.014 quadrillion ($39.3 billion) on public investment this year, with roads, airports and other infrastructure under construction nationwide. Indonesia's growth, by contrast, has hovered around 5%. The IMF forecasts 5.1% for the country this year, against 8.4% for Vietnam. Vietnam is targeting growth of at least 10% this year and aims to lift GDP per capita to about $8,500 by 2030, roughly Thailand's level today. Fujita said Vietnam also needs to pursue long-term growth by developing human resources and technology, alongside the infrastructure spending that lifts growth in the short term.

picked.t: [베트남 경제동향] 올해 1인당 GDP 인도네시아 추월 전망...동남아 경제 판도 변화
picked.body: 베트남의 산업단지에서 전자제품 및 제조업 생산이 진행되고 있다. 첨단 제조업 육성과 외국인 투자 확대는 베트남 경제성장의 주요 동력으로 꼽힌다. (사진=베트남 연합뉴스통신) (호치민=베트남코리아타임즈) 반 린 (Van Linh) 기자 = 베트남의 1인당 국내총생산(GDP)이 올해 인도네시아를 넘어설 것으로 전망됐다. 베트남이 그동안 인도네시아에 뒤처졌던 1인당 GDP에서 역전에 성공할 것으로 예상되면서 동남아시아 주요 경제국 간 경제구도에도 변화가 나타날 전망이다. 국제통화기금(IMF)이 지난 10월 발표한 세계경제전망(WEO)에 따르면 베트남의 올해 명목 1인당 GDP는 5,259달러로 예상됐다. 이는 지난해보다 8.9% 증가한 수준으로, 인도네시아의 예상치인 5,153달러를 106달러 웃도는 규모다. 베트남의 1인당 GDP는 2025년 4,829달러로 인도네시아의 5,078달러보다 낮았다. 그러나 올해 베트남 경제가 상대적으로 빠른 성장세를 보이면서 양국 간 순위가 뒤바뀔 것으로 전망됐다. 이번 전망이 현실화하면 베트남은 싱가포르, 브루나이, 말레이시아, 태국에 이어 아세안(ASEAN) 회원국 가운데 1인당 GDP 5위에 오르게 된다. IMF는 베트남의 1인당 GDP가 2027년 5,659달러로 상승해 인도네시아의 5,550달러를 계속 웃돌 것으로 예상했다. 다만 전체 경제 규모에서는 인도네시아가 여전히 베트남을 크게 앞서고 있다. 인도네시아의 올해 명목 GDP는 1조4,800억달러로 예상되는 반면 베트남은 5,420억달러 수준에 그칠 전망이다. 인도네시아의 인구가 약 2억9,000만명으로 베트남의 1억명보다 훨씬 많기 때문이다.   첨단 제조업과 인프라 투자가 성장 견인 베트남의 1인당 GDP 상승에는 제조업 고도화와 외국인 투자 확대, 정부의 적극적인 공공투자 등이 영향을 미친 것으로 분석된다. 특히 반도체와 전자제품 등 첨단 제조업 분야에서 베트남의 역할이 확대되고 있다. 대만 폭스콘(Foxconn)이 베트남 내 생산시설을 확대하고 있으며, 한국 삼성전자도 북부 지역 공장을 중심으로 스마트폰과 전자제품을 생산해 세계 시장에 공급하고 있다. 정부의 대규모 인프라 투자 역시 경제성장을 뒷받침하고 있다. 베트남은 올해 도로와 공항 등 국가 기반시설 확충을 위해 1,014조동(약 393억달러)을 공공투자에 투입할 계획이다. 전국적으로 고속도로와 공항 등 대형 인프라 사업이 진행되면서 건설 및 관련 산업의 성장에도 기여하고 있다. 경제성장률에서도 양국 간 차이가 두드러진다. IMF는 올해 베트남의 경제성장률을 8.4%로 전망한 반면 인도네시아는 5.1%로 예상했다. 베트남은 올해 3분기 국내총생산(GDP)이 전년 동기 대비 9.95% 증가해 최근 4년 사이 가장 높은 분기 성장률을 기록했다. 베트남 정부는 올해 경제성장률 목표를 최소 10%로 설정하고 있으며, 2030년까지 1인당 GDP를 약 8,500달러로 끌어올린다는 목표도 제시했다. 다만 1인당 GDP 순위 역전이 곧바로 국민의 실질적인 생활수준 역전을 의미하는 것은 아니다. 이번 전망은 물가 변동을 조정하지 않은 명목 GDP를 기준으로 하며, 달러 환산 과정에서 환율 변동도 영향을 미친다. 베트남이 향후 지속적인 성장세를 유지하기 위해서는 인프라 확충과 외국인 투자 유치뿐 아니라 노동생산성 향상, 기술 개발, 고급 인력 양성 등 산업 경쟁력을 높이기 위한 과제도 해결해야 한다. 베트남이 첨단 제조업 육성과 산업구조 고도화를 통해 동남아시아 주요 경제국으로서 입지를 얼마나 확대할 수 있을지 주목된다.   <저작권자(c) 베트남코리아타임즈, 무단 전재-재배포 금지>

picked.t: The Coca-Cola Foundation, IUCN seek business opportunities in ecosystem restoration
picked.body: The Coca-Cola Foundation (TCCF) and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) presented business opportunities linked to ecosystem restoration at the 2026 Autumn Economic Forum in Ho Chi Minh City on Oct. 27. At a panel discussion titled "Turning ecosystem restoration into scalable business opportunities," the organizations showcased nature-based solutions that combine conservation with economic activities in the Mekong Delta. The discussion, held at the Rising Star Arena – Technology and Innovation Showcase, brought together stakeholders to explore ways to attract investment and generate income for local communities through restoration projects. The Mekong Delta faces coastal erosion, mangrove loss, disrupted seasonal flooding, excessive groundwater extraction and land subsidence, threatening agricultural production and local livelihoods. Since 2017, TCCF, the philanthropic arm of The Coca-Cola Company, has provided more than US$1.8 million to support IUCN projects linking ecosystem restoration with agriculture and market opportunities. One initiative promotes flood-based agriculture, combining lotus cultivation, aquaculture and tourism as alternatives to a third annual rice crop. Farmers can use seasonal floodwaters to produce lotus-based food, fiber, textiles and artwork, while generating income from aquaculture and tourism. Another model combines mangrove restoration with integrated multi-trophic aquaculture and recirculating aquaculture systems (IMTA-RAS). It integrates conservation with aquaculture technology to maintain production, improve water-use efficiency and quality, and strengthen coastal resilience. The organizations said scaling up these models would require commercially viable projects, measurable outcomes, partnerships and access to finance. Blended finance, which combines public and commercial funding, could help attract investment. Public funding can support project preparation, technical assistance, implementation and monitoring, while private capital can finance investments and expansion. IUCN and TCCF said they aimed to strengthen cooperation among businesses, public agencies and other stakeholders to mobilize resources for sustainable development in the Mekong Delta. TCCF also supports other environmental initiatives in Vietnam. Since 2007, it has worked with WWF-Viet Nam on biodiversity conservation and natural water regulation at Tram Chim National Park, committing an additional $500,000 for 2024–2027. The foundation also partners with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) on the Ending Plastic Waste Innovation Programme, which supports local waste management solutions. The program has incubated and accelerated 11 innovation projects and supported efforts to prevent or recycle more than 750 tonnes of plastic waste, while seeking to improve livelihoods for waste management workers.

picked.t: Foreign employers in Vietnam face new hiring duties from November
picked.body: The government decree effective on Nov. 15 requires foreign organizations and individuals that need Vietnamese workers to notify the managing agency or organization in writing, by post or online via its official email, specifying the job position and headcount. Foreign organizations and individuals must also publicly post recruitment information for Vietnamese workers on the National Employment Exchange at https://vieclam.gov.vn/, other lawful job portals or their own official website. They must recruit Vietnamese workers directly. At their request, the managing agency or organization will select and refer candidates based on the job description provided. Under the decree, they must notify the managing agency or organization in writing, by post or online via its official email within 10 working days of signing a labor contract with a Vietnamese worker, stating the worker's full name, personal identification number, job position and start date. Other decrees effective next month set out 15 groups of investment and business sectors subject to security and order conditions, administrative penalties for lottery business and data, and new rules on automobile use standards and norms, universal preschool education for children aged 5- 6, compulsory education and literacy.

picked.t: Old growth model cannot make Vietnam rich: World Bank official
picked.body: Vietnam needs a new growth model focused on productivity and better jobs to achieve high-income status by 2045, according to Mariam J. Sherman, World Bank country director for Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. Speaking at the U.K.-Vietnam Business Forum in Ho Chi Minh City on Oct. 29, Sherman said the country had made major progress since the Doi Moi (Renovation) reforms, rising from one of the world's poorest nations to an upper-middle-income economy. GDP per capita has increased sixfold to more than US$5,000, driven by trade liberalization, foreign investment, the shift of workers from agriculture to manufacturing and capital accumulation. Vietnam's capital stock has doubled about every 6.5 years. "But the formula that brought Vietnam to where it is today will not take it to high-income status," Sherman said, warning that the country's three main growth drivers — a large workforce, rapid capital accumulation and deeper trade integration — were nearing their limits. Vietnam's working-age population peaked in 2014, while the share of people aged over 65 is projected to double to 14% by 2035. The country risks growing old before becoming rich, making productivity gains increasingly important, Sherman said. A manufacturing worker in Vietnam generates about $6.70 in value added per hour, less than half the level in China. Sherman also described a "dual economy," in which foreign-invested companies account for 73% of exports and generally have higher productivity and wages than domestic firms, while links between the two sectors remain limited. "This is the heart of the challenge. Vietnam's exports have become more sophisticated, but jobs for Vietnamese workers have not kept pace," she said. Four priorities for the next growth phase The World Bank has identified four priorities to help Vietnam reach high-income status by 2045. The first is to improve job quality and close the skills gap, particularly in digital and technical fields. The rise of artificial intelligence makes it more urgent to align education and training with labor market needs, Sherman said. The second is to improve connections between markets, people and regions. High logistics costs and pressure on electricity supplies highlight the need for transport and energy infrastructure upgrades, which the World Bank estimates will require about $400 billion. The third is to turn climate risks into economic opportunities. Vietnam is highly vulnerable to climate change, which could reduce GDP by 12.5% by 2050 without adequate action. Its energy intensity is twice the East Asian average, while emissions linked to exports account for more than a third of national emissions. A well-designed decarbonization strategy could increase GDP by nearly 3% by 2040, according to the World Bank. The fourth priority is institutional reform. Sherman said the government needed to shift from directly planning and producing to enabling and regulating economic activity as the economy becomes more complex and innovation-driven. British Ambassador to Vietnam Iain Frew said the global economy was undergoing major changes, with the shift to cleaner energy creating new industries and geopolitical developments highlighting the need for resilience and reliable partnerships. He said Vietnam's Resolution 68 on private sector development, Resolution 57 on science, technology and innovation, and Resolution 10 on attracting high-quality investment set out an ambitious vision for the country's next growth phase. The U.K. is ready to support Vietnam in capital market development, workforce training, technology, innovation and green growth, he added. Bilateral trade in goods and services has reached £10.5 billion (US$13.9 billion), double the 2020 level. The U.K.-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement and both countries' membership in the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) are creating business opportunities by reducing trade barriers and helping diversify supply chains, Frew said. Denzel Eades, chairman of BritCham, called Vietnam's economic transformation "one of Asia's most impressive growth stories" and said British investors were committed to expanding their presence in the country. "With our strengths in finance, innovation, education, and sustainability, we look forward to working with the government and industry partners to help realize Vietnam's vision of becoming a prosperous, high-value, and globally connected economy by 2045," he said. The U.K.-Vietnam Business Forum, BritCham's largest annual economic dialogue, was held in partnership with the Ho Chi Minh City Center for the Fourth Industrial Revolution (HCMC C4IR) as part of the 2026 Autumn Economic Forum.

picked.t: Vietnam trade crosses $1 trillion for first time
picked.body: Exports have been worth $493 billion, up 27.2% year-on-year. Imports are up 37.6% to nearly $508 billion, according to the customs department. The trade figure has gone past full-year 2025’s $930 billion with two months to spare. With imports growing faster than exports, the trade deficit was $14.02 billion. The department forecast exports to rise by more than 25% for the full year, well above the government’s target of 15-16%. In 2007, when the country joined the World Trade Organization, its trade had been $100 billion. Growth this year has been driven mainly by foreign-owned companies, who accounted for $778 billion of the trade figure, up 37% from a year earlier. Domestic companies recorded $223 billion, a 16% rise. The three largest traded items were computers, electronic products and their components; phones and components; and machinery, equipment, tools, and spare parts. China and the U.S. remained Vietnam’s two largest trading partners. Exports to several markets with which Vietnam has free trade agreements rose sharply, including Mexico, up 42.5%, South Korea (19.1%), Japan (18.6%), and Canada (14.4%). Vietnam now has trade ties with 237 countries and territories. The Ministry of Industry and Trade is drafting a strategy for goods imports and exports through 2030, with diversifying markets being a priority. It wants to ensure that no single market accounts for more than 25% of total exports or 35% of imports by 2030. The combined share of the three largest export markets or regions will be capped at 55%. For the fourth quarter, the Ministry of Industry and Trade plans to focus on utilizing free trade agreements, expanding markets, and improving companies’ capability to comply with regulations. Measures include early warnings about trade remedy cases, tariff barriers, green standards, traceability requirements, and rules of origin. The ministry also plans to promote formal exports, expand agreements and protocols for agricultural quarantine, invest in cold-chain logistics, and standardize growing areas and packing facilities to meet the global market’s requirements.

picked.t: Moroccan student's journey from knowing only the local words for 'hello' to becoming Vietnam's top maritime navigation graduate
picked.body: A photograph of 23-year-old Moroccan student Hiba Faradji beaming as she accepted a top graduate award at Vietnam Maritime University in August quickly went viral across social media. However, behind this picture-perfect moment of triumph lies a deeply turbulent and emotionally taxing journey that nearly derailed her academic dreams. Her story began at the age of 18, when Faradji left her coastal hometown of Tangier, Morocco. Armed with a prestigious medical scholarship, she relocated to France to begin her studies at the renowned Sorbonne University in Paris. Unfortunately, her arrival coincided with the sudden, global outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic. The unprecedented health crisis immediately threw her academic plans into chaos. Her coursework became increasingly difficult to manage, and her living situation grew highly unstable. Forced to repeatedly stay with acquaintances far from the university campus, Faradji simultaneously battled a series of personal setbacks. After enduring eight months of stress and isolation, the overwhelmed student made the difficult decision to abandon her medical studies entirely and return to Morocco, facing a highly uncertain future. Deeply discouraged by the setback, Faradji isolated herself at home for nearly seven months. The once-outgoing student found herself battling depression, withdrawing completely from the outside world and plagued by a constant fear of being controlled by others. As her mental health gradually stabilized, she resumed her search for international education programs. However, she quickly faced a new wave of obstacles, enduring repeated rejections from universities in both Spain and South Korea. In late 2022, just as she was feeling entirely out of options, a lifeline emerged. Faradji stumbled upon an announcement for four full academic scholarships being offered by the Vietnam Maritime University. Seeking a way out of her predicament, she applied for the university’s bachelor’s program in maritime navigation, encouraged by the full scholarship. Her family supported the decision, and a close friend of her mother even helped pay for her plane ticket. "I had very little time to prepare or learn about Vietnam. I just thought Hai Phong might be similar to my hometown, a coastal city that was neither too big nor too remote," Faradji recalled. Her first day in Vietnam was yet another memorable experience. In February 2023, Faradji arrived at Hanoi's Noi Bai International Airport just before the Lunar New Year, Vietnam's largest national holiday and the most important occasion for family reunion. With passenger buses practically unavailable during the peak travel season, she had little choice but to spend VND2.5 million (US$97), half the total cash she was carrying along at that moment, on a direct taxi to Hai Phong. She arrived to find her cold dormitory completely deserted, as local students had already left for their hometowns for the holiday, leaving her on the verge of tears and wishing she could fly straight back home. As her parents called to check on her, Faradji pulled herself together and told herself she had to keep going. Challenges continued Although she had a strong command of English and French, Faradji found her coursework "quite difficult" because of the specialized terminology and calculations involved. "Math has never been my strength, while Ship Stability is highly detailed and technical. It was so difficult that I could not cover the entire curriculum in just two semesters," she said. To overcome difficulties, she spent considerable time studying independently at home to keep up. She identified her biggest challenges as the psychological wounds she had carried from Paris, differences in daily life in a new environment, and being one of the few female students in a predominantly male department. As a Muslim, Faradji strictly avoids pork. During her first three months in Hai Phong, before becoming accustomed to local cuisine, she subsisted largely on nuts and dried foods sent by her mother. Poor nutrition caused her to lose 4 kg and suffer from prolonged insomnia. Language was another obstacle. Initially, she knew only one Vietnamese phrase: "xin chao," meaning "hello." After five months of basic Vietnamese lessons, combined with observing and imitating the people around her, she gradually became more confident. A turning point came when Faradji joined an English club, where she befriended a student named Thuy, who invited her to stay with her family. This gave Faradji an opportunity to practice speaking Vietnamese in everyday situations. She eventually became familiar even with distinctive expressions and speech patterns used by people in Hai Phong. Once she settled into her studies, Faradji began supporting herself by taking part-time jobs and renting her own apartment. picked.t: South Korea's foreign residents hit record 2.66 million as international student numbers soar
picked.body: The Ministry of the Interior and Safety counted a record 2,662,967 foreign residents as of Nov. 1, 2025, up 79,341, or 3.1%, from a year earlier, The Korea Times reported, citing a ministry report released on Oct. 28. It was the fourth straight annual rise. Foreign residents now made up 5.1% of the country's population of more than 51.8 million. The tally covers people who have lived in South Korea for more than 90 days. It comprises 2,109,057 foreign nationals, 256,491 naturalized Korean citizens and 297,419 Korean-born children of foreign residents. International students posted the steepest growth of any group, rising 17.6% to 274,329. Foreign workers grew 2.3% to 514,043 and marriage immigrants 1.1% to 194,017, while ethnic Koreans holding foreign nationality fell 1.1% to 411,314. Vietnamese were the second largest group among residents without Korean citizenship, at 318,090, or 15.1%, behind Chinese nationals of Korean descent at 534,520, The Korea Economic Daily reported. Other Chinese nationals numbered 220,775 and Thais 158,547. People of Vietnamese origin also made up 23.7% of those who had acquired Korean citizenship, second only to Chinese of Korean descent, the newspaper said. Among international students, though, Vietnam overtook China as the largest group in South Korean higher education as of April this year, with 96,834 students, or 31.5% of the total, according to Education Ministry data released in August. Foreign residents increased in all 17 provinces and metropolitan cities, Korea JoongAng Daily reported, with North Gyeongsang posting the fastest growth at 8%, followed by Gangwon at 7.9%. Gyeonggi, the province surrounding Seoul, had the largest foreign population at 859,943, followed by Seoul at 453,201. The greater Seoul area was home to 1,487,968 foreign residents, or 55.9% of the total. At the municipal level, Ansan in Gyeonggi led with 109,544 foreign residents, followed by Hwaseong, Siheung, Suwon and Bucheon, all also in the province. South Chungcheong had the highest foreign share of any province or metropolitan city at 7.9%, while in the southwestern county of Yeongam foreign residents made up 22.4% of the population, the highest of any locality, The Korea Economic Daily reported. The number of cities, counties and districts with a high concentration of foreign residents, defined as those with at least 10,000 foreign residents or a foreign share of 5% or more, rose by 12 to 154. Jang Heon-beom, director general of the Interior Ministry's Local Administration Bureau, said the increase "shows that local communities are becoming more diverse and dynamic," Korea JoongAng Daily reported. He said the data would help shape policies that allow foreign residents to settle stably into local communities.

picked.t: Travel + Leisure, Lonely Planet recommend November visits to Ha Long
picked.body: November is among the recommended months to visit Ha Long Bay in northern Vietnam, according to international travel publications Travel + Leisure and Lonely Planet . In an article updated on Oct. 11, Travel + Leisure listed April, October and November as suitable months for cruising the UNESCO World Heritage Site, when weather is generally warm, sunny and dry. Lonely Planet also recommends October and November for visiting Ha Long Bay and neighboring Bai Tu Long Bay, citing mild temperatures and a greater likelihood of dry weather. The conditions are suitable for exploring the bay's limestone formations, caves and islands by boat or kayak. Travel + Leisure also recommends overnight cruises, which allow visitors to spend more time exploring the bay and see its scenery at different times of day. Trips typically include afternoon sightseeing, dinner on board and an overnight stay. Beyond cruises, visitors can explore attractions in Bai Chay, one of Ha Long's main tourism areas. Ha Long International Cruise Port, developed by Sun Group, serves cruise passengers and is close to hotels, restaurants and entertainment facilities. At Sun World Ha Long, the Queen Cable Car crosses the entrance to Cua Luc Bay, offering views of Bai Chay Bridge, the waterfront and surrounding urban areas. It connects to Ba Deo Hill, which features a Japanese-style garden with koi ponds, black pine trees and walking paths. Bai Chay also has dining and entertainment options for visitors in the evening. Vui-Fest Ha Long, in the Lighthouse area, features street food, shopping and entertainment, while Sun Bavaria Ha Long offers dining options for families and groups. For visitors seeking wellness activities, Quang Hanh offers hot-spring experiences amid a mountainous landscape. Hilton Quang Hanh Onsen Resort provides accommodation with private hot-spring bathing facilities, while the area's natural mineral springs offer an option for relaxation during the cooler months. With cruises, cable-car rides, dining venues and hot-spring facilities, Ha Long offers visitors several options for November trips. The recommendations from Travel + Leisure and Lonely Planet highlight the bay's seasonal conditions, while nearby attractions provide additional activities beyond sightseeing on the water.
